speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43 I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity arising out of recent press reports that the major oil companies have notified the Anti-Inflation Board of their intention to raise retail gasoline prices as of March 1 by about 3.5 cents per gallon, even though increased wellhead prices for crude oil would only justify about 2.3 cents. In light of the fact that this extra increase in price would net the oil companies an extra $78 million in revenues, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the government take the necessary steps to forbid the rise in retail gasoline prices by any more than is justified by the recent increase in wellhead prices for crude oil.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the question has been discussed by the government, both with the labour side and with the corporate sector. I think it would clearly be desirable to return to a situation where the organized labour movement takes an active and responsible participation in the canvassing of broader public issues in Canada. For my part, if arrangements can be established to have such consultations on a multipartite basis, I think it would be very desirable. Obviously, whether or not this will be done, either in the near future or with the labour movement, will depend very much on the outcome of discussions on Monday. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance deliberately used the word "multipartite". subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF COMMENCING TRIPARTITE DISCUSSIONS OF ECONOMIC POLICY-GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no new institution is involved in this respect, unless one regards a meeting between two or more parties as being of an institutional character. There is no definitive proposal in this regard. What we would propose would be to discuss the circumstances under

which organized labour would really be prepared to come back into discussions with the other major decision makers in the economy. For this purpose "multipartite" would include not only organized labour and the management side, but also, because of the nature of our federalism, should include the provincial governments as well. Concepts very much along that same line will, of course, take place with the provinces in the following days at the meeting of the finance ministers.

subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF COMMENCING TRIPARTITE DISCUSSIONS OF ECONOMIC POLICY-GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in effect the Minister of Finance is admitting the failure of the process of separate consultations with separate groups, which was the process undertaken by his predecessor as Minister of Finance. He indicates he will be holding discussions regarding new methods or models with the CLC, the Canadian Manufacturer's Association and with the provinces. I wonder if the minister plans to come before the House of Commons with an indication of the models the government has in mind for subsequent discussion of national social and economic goals on which Final decisions have to be taken by this body?

subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF COMMENCING TRIPARTITE DISCUSSIONS OF ECONOMIC POLICY-GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, indeed I think it would be most appropriate to have effective House discussion on this question. We are approaching it in the mood of saying we think it is desirable that there be this continuing communication among the major decision makers in our economy, and we would like to know under those circumstances how they envisage future participation of the private sector, whether labour or management, in the kind of decisions that governments, and I use that word in the plural, have to make about the Canadian economy.

subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF COMMENCING TRIPARTITE DISCUSSIONS OF ECONOMIC POLICY-GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, is the Minister of Finance telling us that the government of Canada is going into these discussions with the other partners in the Canadian economy with nothing on its own mind and no model of its own to propose, and that it is simply going to rely upon the other partners to propose what they think is desirable, as it has been relying upon the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, for example, to initiate discussions on post-controls policy, and as it is relying upon the CMA and the CLC to propose some form that will work better than the process that has been followed to this point of separate consultation? subsubtopic: POSSIBILITY OF COMMENCING TRIPARTITE DISCUSSIONS OF ECONOMIC POLICY-GOVERNMENT PROPOSALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have discussed very extensively with the public what kind of proposal we think can be effective. For example, the hon. member and I yesterday exchanged some viewpoints on the possibility of a monitoring institution in the post-controls period. It would be a faulty conclusion for the Leader of the Opposition to say that we are going in without some proposals in our own mind which, in due

course, after sounding out the various parties, will certainly be solidified. The intelligent way-surely, in this regard, instead of the way the Leader of the Opposition would follow, saying this is it; that is all-is to talk about the problem, talk about some alternative approaches that can be taken and, indeed, to have a genuine dialogue with those who are involved.

The House resumed from, Thursday, January 27, consideration of the motion of Mr. Macdonald (Rosedale) that Bill C-21, to amend the Excise Tax Act, be read the second time and referred to committee of the whole.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to bring a number of matters to the attention of the minister. My reason for doing so at this point is to allow him the opportunity to look into the remarks I am about to make and provide me with answers at some appropriate time as the bill proceeds. One of the questions I wish to raise with the minister is this. As we know, he has had to back away from the position he originally took in trying to promote energy conservation through a measure depending upon the weight of cars. He is considering whether it is not more appropriate to impose penalties based on the mileage per gallon or lack of mileage per gallon achieved.
I wonder whether the minister has done any research in a similar direction to determine whether the penalty on air-conditioners might not be counterproductive. The understanding given to us in defence of the imposition of a tax on air-conditioners was that they consume a tremendous amount of energy. This seemed a plausible argument and one which we on this side are prepared to support if it will, indeed, result in conservation. However, representations have been made to me suggesting that in fact air-conditioners might not be especially important in terms of energy consumption.

January 28, 1977
Excise Tax Act
I should like to read the following letter to the House and ask the minister to reply to it at an appropriate time. The letter is from Dave's Auto Radio, of Kitchener. It is headed "Re: Bill C-21, automotive air-conditioner tax", and reads as follows:
The proposed purpose of taxing automotive air-conditioners is to encourage people to conserve energy. This is based on the assumption that car air-conditioner units are a heavy user of fuel.
I feel that this is only the case air-conditioning units that operate all the time such as GM's Comfortron. All manual air-conditioners operate only when needed and then only intermittently. These units are thermostatically controlled and as soon as the car's interior reaches the desired temperature, the compressor shuts off.
To be more specific on consumption of fuel, it is a well known fact that a car with the windows down on a hot day will consume as much, or more, fuel than a car with air-conditioning and the windows up. This is because when the windows are down, the car is subject to wind drag. When windows are up, it presents a clean entry into the air.
I believe that you and other MPs are being misled and poorly informed on this matter.
The letter is signed by Mr. Johnson. I do not have at my disposal the kind of research that would be required to know whether the arguments being put forward in the letter are as stated, but I think this is a very important matter. Since the question has been raised and the minister has had to reconsider some of his other approaches to fuel consumption, such as the weight of cars, the minister should tell the House what kind of research has been carried out on air-conditioners and what happens to fuel consumption. Have the facts put forward in the letter been examined, and what conclusions has the department come to?
Another matter I should like to raise at this time has to do with a letter sent to the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) from the Canadian Council of Rehabilitation Workshops. The president, Mr. Les Gray, asked the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre to have this matter raised in the House when the Excise Tax Act came up for examination, so this seems to me the appropriate time to raise it. I think I could best put the argument in the form in which it appears in the letter, and I will quote directly from the letter and ask the minister what is being done in this regard. At the conclusion of the letter there is some indication that the matter is under study, and once again I should like the minister to report at the appropriate time what the studies have revealed and what conclusions the government has come to in terms of making a policy decision. The letter is addressed to the Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin) and reads in part:
The purpose of this letter is to bring to your attention certain exclusions in the guidelines under the federal Excise Tax Act related to exemptions of federal sales tax for institutions and facilities whose prime objective is the rehabilitation of handicapped or disadvantaged persons.
A number of the workshops or rehabilitation facilities in Canada are not involved in activities that produce an item that would be considered under the act. Specifically this would be the renovating or refurbishing of items for resale such as clothing, electrical appliances, furniture, etc. In the course of these

activities they must utilize various supplies and equipment to carry out this function, some of these being dry-cleaning fluid, soaps, buttons, paint, nails, electrical wiring, various tools and machinery such as washers, saws, drill presses, etc. that they must purchase and are charged federal sales tax.
The market segment for these goods is extremely selective and economically depressed causing a very low margin of return for the facilities who in turn must reflect this in the payment to the workers, retarding any incentive that may be generated, thereby in large measure defeating the rehabilitative goals of the facility. Being exempt from federal sales tax would greatly assist these facilities in achieving their objectives.
A further consideration is in the area of federal sales tax that is charged in the purchase of building materials for new construction or renovation of the previously mentioned facilities. The current costs of construction have made expansion in this respect extremely limited and I would ask that consideration be given to the exemption of the facility in these purchases or by some means applicable to the contractor.
The third matter of consideration is to a change in the guidelines related to the certification of institutions so as to encompass the broad spectrum of persons that we attempt to rehabilitate. At present, under the strict interpretations, persons who are socially disadvantaged and others who are in a transitional state following confinement to a penal institution, drug or alcoholic treatment centre and who make up the majority of persons in a given facility are not covered in the certification authority granting that facility exemptions of sales tax in production or purchase of materials and equipment.
It would be difficult to determine the exact amount of revenue that would be lost if these proposals were to be acceded to, but I feel it would be very minimal on the scale of the total intake of federal sales tax.
We have been advised that the current guidelines are presently under review and ask that you give the above matter your most serious consideration.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that this, too, is an important matter and for this reason I raise it at this time. Since the matter is under review and we are prepared to make exemptions under the Excise Tax Act regarding certain items of social importance, it is a matter of considerable concern that we know whether the department has come to a conclusion or whether the minister is prepared to grant these exemptions to rehabilitative centres. If some difficulty is caused because there are so many items purchased, then I suggest it is possible from the administrative point of view to institute some kind of rebate or withdrawal system at the end of a purchase period which would reimburse these institutions in respect of sales tax.
I will leave this matter with the minister and give him an opportunity of refreshing his memory or obtaining additional information from his officials, and I would ask him to reply to the two matters I have raised when the bill reaches committee stage.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think it would be proper to comment on Bill C-21, to amend the Excise Tax Act, without taking a brief look, at least, at the history of this excise tax in Canada. I think it is one of the poorer forms of tax which governments over the years have introduced and which this government has perpetuated, added to and changed. I say "poorer form" because it is a hidden tax, the kind of tax that people who pay it really have no knowledge of unless they happen to be versed in the law or business practices. Further, it is a tax that has another tax on it. In

other words, nine of Canada's ten provinces have added a retail sales tax which automatically is increased by this hidden tax known as the Excise Tax. Another poor feature of this tax is the amount of paper work, recording, and so on, which is forced on small businessmen. In fact, it is forced on all businessmen, but it is a greater burden, I am afraid, for small businessmen.
I think the honest policy for the government to take, though I am afraid this government has no intention or perhaps does not have even have the ability or desire to take this kind of tack, would be to replace this kind of tax with some other kind of tax which individuals then know they are paying. I do not know what kind of tax could be substituted, but I should like to put forward one or two ideas. It has been said that a sales tax, particularly this sort of sales tax, is regressive because it is paid equally by rich and poor and has no regard for the situation of the individual who is paying it.
Some four years ago in this House I advocated that the income tax was also an unfair tax and that it should be replaced. At that time I was thinking-in fact, I suggested it to this government-that income tax could easily be replaced by some sort of a consumption tax which would be like a sales tax but need not be hidden and people would know what they were paying. That attracted great criticism from the other side, on the basis that my suggestion was regressive and it would hurt the very people the government wants to help. They cannot have it both ways. They cannot, on the one hand, say that to eliminate the income tax would be regressive, while on the other condoning and in fact supporting a tax such as this excise tax.
It was my contention at the time that exemptions could be granted to help those in lower income ranges to make the purchases everyone has to make of the essentials, which could be exempted from this kind of tax. For example, food is generally exempt now, I believe, and would be exempted from the consumption or sales tax. Other essentials are clothing and housing. The list might be a little bit longer than that, but those are basics and could be exempted.
The critics of my remarks at that time also said that Canada could not get along without an income tax. That is only because we have had governments over the years which have spent themselves into the position where they must have that kind of tax in order to raise the huge revenues they need. 1 would remind the government that Canada got along for 50 years without an income tax-from 1867 until 1917. I would remind it, too, that in 1917 income tax was introduced as a temporary measure to raise funds for the war effort. That went on, as we know, and it was even called the income war tax act until after the next World War, when in 1949 the name of the act changed to reflect its honest purpose and it is now called the Income Tax Act. Just to say the government cannot get along without it because it needs the revenue is not good enough.
Excise Tax Act
The government examines all sorts and manner of things from beginning to end, ad nauseam, and there is no reason at all that the government could not examine other means of raising the revenue it needs. I know we are not debating the Income Tax Act, Mr. Speaker, but I think it is worth while to draw the parallel so the government might be moved to consider some alternate form of revenue or some other treatment of this kind of tax.
The government has often talked about equity and simplicity, as in fact it did in the white paper on income tax. I do not think there is anyone in this House who thinks our tax system is either simple or equitable. This excise tax is just another example of a dishonest way of raising money from the people, because it is a hidden tax. Hidden taxes really cannot be said to be honest types of taxes. Therefore, I am urging that the government take the opportunity it has of using its facilities to make some real studies to find ways to overcome the problems I am raising.
Dealing with the bill itself, the fact that there are things to criticize does not mean it is a bill in which we cannot find some good features. For example, in the minister's statement last night he made reference to the removal of the sales tax from a number of items which contribute to the conservation of energy. I do not think we can argue very much with that. The proposal is to remove the tax from such items as solar furnaces, heat panels, heat pumps and wind-powered generating equipment. Furthermore, the proposal is to extend the current exemption to include thermal insulation materials designed for use in insulating pipes and ducts used in buildings and mechanical systems.
The minister also made reference to the statement tabled by his colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie), entitled "An Energy Strategy for Canada- Policies for Self-reliance". The reference to that paper, I think, led the government to move to the conservation aspects of this bill, many of which are contained in clause 5.
One of these which I think was somewhat unfair was the addition of the $100 tax on air-conditioners when installed in automobiles. There is one particular aspect of that which I think is unfair to the Canadian taxpayer. That is, it was applied retroactively. That is to say, where a valid contract existed on the budget date, the date of that contract was ignored and the tax was applied also to any vehicle that had been purchased or contracted for prior to that date. This completely ignores the fact that a contractual situation existed between the purchaser and the vendor. Through no fault of his own, the purchaser-or the transaction, in any event-was burdened with an additional $100 excise tax.
That may not be a "life or death" proposition for someone who is contracting to spend a lot of money to buy a new vehicle, but it is an example of the fact that this government has chosen, again, to ignore the effect of contracts and apply its penalties to people it probably did not mean to trap in the first place. In any event, that has been explored, and there is no question but that the tax on air-conditioners for vehicles

Clause 5 also refers to a weight tax on automobiles. The idea put forth by the minister undoubtedly is that heavier automobiles use more gasoline and, therefore, they should be taxed to discourage their purchase in order to conserve, in this case, petroleum energy in Canada. However, the minister has presented no statistics to support the argument that this is a desirable form of taxation or a desirable thing to discourage. I do not think I would argue that a heavier vehicle will not burn more gasoline than a lighter vehicle, but that is not the only measure of the use of energy; that is, the amount of gasoline a vehicle may burn. After all, it costs a lot in energy resources to produce a vehicle. I put it this way to the government, that a heavier vehicle may last two or three times as long and may be able to travel two or three times as many miles as a lighter vehicle that is not as well made.
The lighter vehicle may get somewhat better gas mileage and conserve energy in that respect, but if the heavier vehicle lasts twice as long or three times as long as the lighter vehicle, it leads to a real saving of energy; and not only of energy but of resources, because two or three lighter automobiles would need to be produced in order to replace the lighter vehicle which had worn out. 1 do not have the facilities to conduct tests which will prove my argument, but the government has those facilities. I think the government owes it to Canadians to use its extensive research facilities to study what I have been suggesting. It should do it before it imposes a tax which is based on conclusions which may not be accurate.
I shall leave that particular aspect of the matter and mention, before I finish, the aspect of cottage industries. The excise tax set certain limits in the past which at the time were probably realistic but which nowadays are not. Today, many small businesses are struggling to stay alive; struggling, I say, because in most cases these small businesses are not corporations but are run by a proprietor trying to make a living. That proprietor, who may be producing relatively small quantities of goods to sell to consumers, finds himself trapped by the present excise tax limit. He finds that he is included in the $10,000 manufacturing level and a large proportion of his net income must be paid to the government in the form of excise tax. I
I am not saying that the principle is incorrect. After all, many of these people are manufacturers. But this situation is a further example showing that the government has failed to keep pace with what is happening from day to day; has failed to keep pace with the present-day situation. I appeal to the government to stop making band-aid changes to legislation like this, especially to stop making changes which have been insufficiently thought out, because some Canadians are trapped in circumstances they did not design for themselves. I hope there will be some permanent improvement to the system of taxation in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot let a bill on excise tax go by without saying a few words and expressing some of my own sentiments about the excise tax, a tax which I think is probably more unfair than any other type of tax. It really does nothing: especially, it does not do what the government would like to tell the people it does. I said it does not do anything, but it does: it raises lots of money for the government and many people who are paying it do not really know when and how they are paying it.
The discussion paper of June 23, 1975, on federal sales and excise taxes set out a number of criteria for an effective sales tax, namely, an optimum blend of neutrality, flexibility and efficiency. The paper finally recognized that the tax is not exclusively a revenue source but is an effective means of influencing consumption and resource utilization in accordance with policy goals. I do not agree with those assumptions. How can a hidden tax influence consumption and resource utilization? It is put on at the manufacturing level and people do not realize or recognize they are paying the tax. It is not put on in front of them; it is hidden. If it were put on at the retail level, I am sure retailers would make certain that consumers knew what tax they were paying-and I am sure this would make the government very unpopular.
I do not think consumers would like it if they realized, every time they bought something, just how much excise for federal sales tax was put on the item, especially considering the percentage rates now charged. Therefore, I cannot agree with the philosophy of the paper regarding resource utilization. I do not think this type of tax helps very much to influence resource utilization, especially since the people do not know what tax they are paying and why they are paying it. As I have said, it certainly raises a great deal of money for the government. It would appear to me, from a study of the schedules of excise tax, that the tax is put on those goods which the government feels will be easy marks and about which the people will not get too upset. About the only time people realize the tax is being put on is at times like this when we have the opportunity to tell them exactly what is going on. Only then do they know.
Many logical briefs were presented to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) in the past year in support of changes to the excise tax and sales tax, briefs such as the one submitted to the minister by the Canadian Handicrafts Council, which points out many of the inequities affecting Canadian craftsmen. That was a very good brief-but nothing has been done about it. Some craftsmen have to pay the tax, and some do not. Painters and sculptors do not; but silversmiths, leather-craft workers and similar craftsmen must pay the tax. Really, these people are small businessmen. They ply a craft and sell their wares either to supplement income or to make a living. It is the small manufacturer who is caught, who really gets hurt, who really gets confused and who really does not understand what is happening to him.
Small businessmen have to pay the excise tax. Some of them are classed as small manufacturers. Mr. Speaker, there is a limit today of $3,000 which was established over 25 years ago. That limit $3,000 may have been sufficient according to the

January 28, 1977

standards of a long time ago, but it is not good enough now. Surely, in Canada, we want to encourage as many people as possible to work for themselves and to start small businesses. Surely, it should be one of our goals to encourage people to work for themselves. Surely, craftsmen should be part of this process. They could easily become the big businessmen of tomorrow, but they are discouraged by an innocuous-sounding tax such as this which stands in the way of their getting started.
I think the $3,000 limit is not high enough. It should be raised to at least $15,000, which would give these types of people an opportunity to start in business and buy the materials they need to become manufacturers and make a living. This is the sort of thing that we should encourage in Canada. Too much has happened in this country in the last few years to drive businessmen and manufacturers out of Canada. They have not been given sufficient opportunities to get started here.
A person who comes to my mind is a pipe manufacturer in my riding who has a business the profits of which are limited to a sufficient amount to allow him to make a living. But this excise tax takes away 12 per cent, which is a large amount for such a small business. He could start the same business in the United States where there is no excise tax, and from there supply the Canadian market. That would not be very good for this country; we would lose a citizen and a manufacturer.
Another nan in my riding who has a small business of his own is making an excellent product, namely, toys. He is struggling to get ahead. But, now, not only does he have to pay the excise tax but he has to do all the paper work as well. It is discouraging to those people, many of whom give up and say to themselves that if they cannot get started in Canada, if they are to be inhibited at every turn, it is easier for them to go on welfare. That is not the way people should talk. We should encourage Canadians to start their own businesses. I say that the small businessman or manufacturer today can have a big business tomorrow. Let us give these people a lot of encouragement.
The fact that this tax will be taken off solar-heat component parts will encourage the development of this source of energy in Canada. That is good and timely. However, if the minister remembers, I have sent him letters regarding the 12 per cent tax on wood stoves. Stoves which use gas or oil, non renewable resources, are not taxed. We have a good supply of wood in many parts of Canada: it is a renewable resource. We are not using wood stoves to any large degree at present, but in the not too distant future we will be using them. I do not know why the tax was imposed in the first place. Perhaps at one time it was put on to encourage people not to use wood but to use oil and electricity. This decision is back-firing today. I think the department should take a long look at the imposition of a tax the result of which is to discourage people from proper resource utilization.
Not long ago the former minister of finance imposed a 10 per cent tax on aircraft, reportedly because of the high fuel
Excise Tax Act
consumption of aircraft. Yet the small aircraft does not use as much fuel as a car. I have a letter here telling me about a businessman in Calgary who has to use his aircraft to go to Drumheller. It is a C-172 Skyhawk. He uses $2.93 worth of fuel. If he took his car, a Cougar XL, he would spend $16 on fuel. That is a tremendous difference. There is a doctor in my riding, in the town of Kelowna, who uses his aircraft to fly to Vancouver. It saves him time and fuel and it is a much better mode of transportation than a car. Perhaps he should fly on scheduled airlines, but the schedule of the airlines does not fit in with his schedules. If he went on a scheduled airline he would have to stay overnight in Vancouver, but when he uses his own aircraft he can go down and back in the same day and he uses much less fuel than if he travelled by car.
Another point I would like to make is that many different taxes are put on small aircraft, such as the sales tax, the user tax and the user-pay tax at airports, all of which discourage the use of this type of transportation. You can buy an aeroplane for the same price that you can buy a car. Therefore, people should be encouraged to use aircraft. If you really want to know the reason the government puts a tax on aeroplanes, it is that aeroplanes are very popular with most people, although not many use them. This is not the type of reasoning that should be behind the imposition of the excise tax.
Before concluding I would like to make a few remarks about the 10 cent gas tax which was put on by the government. I spoke against it at the time. It has been on now for around a year and a half. It is a hidden tax; people do not realize it is there. I bet it has not stopped people using a half a gallon of gasoline more. They are using just as much gas. People do not know about the tax when they go to the gas pump, and it is costing the government plenty of money to collect it. In some instances people are allowed a rebate on the tax, which means costly paper work. This proposed tax will not solve the problem which the government suggests it will. The government should look at other ways of solving this problem so that people will understand what the government is trying to do. A gas tax is not the right way; its purpose is to raise more money for the government. All it has done is just that-raise more money for the government.
Granted, farmers, fishermen and ranchers get a rebate, but only if they take the time to fill in the necessary forms and send them in. Quite a few farmers and ranchers are not doing that and the government is getting a free ride; but this is a cost to farmers and ranchers. If this government really wants to do something for them, it will take the tax off purple gas. It should not have been imposed in the first place. If the government really wants to do something for them, it will put a stop to all the paper work. Then everyone would benefit without having to file for a rebate. However, I do not think that is the main issue. I do not think the tax should be there at all. I think it is an unfair tax. If the provinces want to impose a tax, they can justify it by using the money for building roads and things of that sort. That is a different matter. But the federal government should not be imposing this tax.

Mr. Speaker, I begin my remarks on second reading of Bill C-21 by putting a question to the House and to the minister concerning changes that he appears to have made, and which he referred to yesterday, in the bill compared to the ways and means motion produced on May 25 when the minister's budget was first introduced. In this connection I would point out that yesterday, as reported at page 2478 of Hansard, the minister mentioned that they were in a bit of a quandary as to whether they had hit upon the right energy conservation formula; namely, was it correct to assume that the weight of an automobile was the only gauge as to whether it was a heavy energy user? To that end the department seems to have been sufficiently persuaded that their original proposal of May 25 was not adequate. The minister said:
As a result of these discussions the government has been persuaded that an alternative form of tax based on vehicle fuel consumption rather than weight should be explored further by the industry and those within the government with responsibility for energy conservation.
To provide sufficient time for an in-depth study of this alternative, it was decided that the impact of the proposed tax changes should be reduced. For this reason the bill provides for a reduction of 75 pounds in the automobile weight limit and a reduction of 100 pounds in the weight limit for station wagons and vans, rather than-
I emphasize this:
-the reductions of 250 and 350 pounds respectively proposed in the May 25 budget speech. The reductions in the weight limits and the increases in rate of tax applicable to vehicles in excess of the weight limits are effective as of September 1, 1976. The further reductions in the weight threshold proposed in the May budget to come into effect in 1977 through 1979 will not be implemented at this time.
I draw hon. members attention to that reference by the minister. If hon. members review the ways and means motion and compare it with the provisions that are in the bill before us, they will see quite clearly what the minister is referring to. In the motion that was before us on budget night, for example,

an automobile was taken as having a current structure weight or weight threshold level of 4,500 pounds. It was then proposed that the threshold level be reduced, starting in 1976, to 4,250 pounds and then dropping year by year, until 1979, to 3,500 pounds. Likewise, station wagons were to have a current structure of 5,100 pounds, to be reduced to 4,750 pounds by 1976 and eventually to 3,700 pounds in 1979.
As I read the bill before us, the government is suggesting that the weight no* be reduced to 4,250 pounds, as I indicated was the 1976 figure, but be reduced only to 4,425 pounds. That is to say, the 75 pounds to which the minister has referred, and all the subsequent years reductions that were contemplated for 1977 through to 1979, simply will not be put into effect. My point is simply this, and I guess this is a point of order: can this type of variance between the ways and means motion and the bill be tolerated in the House without having the ways and means motion amended to give effect to the bill that the minister is now proposing?

Then I will continue with more general remarks concerning Bill C-21. I believe it is fair to say that many of the provisions and measures announced in the May budget supporting energy conservation, which at least in part are reflected in this bill, are good. I believe it is also fair to say that they are insufficient to begin the task of getting a grip on the enormous energy problems facing Canadians. Far more encompassing measures apart from elimination of the excise tax on alternate energy hardware is needed if we are to ensure an adequate supply of energy for ourselves and future generations.
The Manitoba chamber of commerce, in a 1976 study on energy policy, stated that Canada surpassed the United States in 1974 and boasted the highest per capita energy consumption
January 28, 1977

of any economy in the world. It was estimated that we would be importing nearly one million barrels a day of oil in 1985 to meet our needs. The study recommended, among other things, increased tax incentives for research and development of alternate sources of energy, as well as incentives to the home owner to encourage conservation of traditional energy sources. The study found that by upgrading thermal performance of insulation, and by improving the efficiency of furnaces, energy consumption in the home could be cut by 15 to 25 per cent.
To encourage the widespread use of these measures the study urged not just the elimination of the federal excise tax on these items but a federal income tax credit on any expenditure to improve the efficiency of home energy consumption. Storm windows and doors, added insulation materials, caulking and weather-stripping materials were among the items which would qualify for a tax credit. As home heating accounts for 60 per cent of all residential energy consumption, the savings resulting from the upgrading of all substandard housing would be considerable-enough to stretch our energy supplies far beyond their expected life. It is projected that we shall be importing one million barrels of oil a day by 1985. At present prices, the importation of oil will cost us around $5 billion annually. The loss of tax revenue resulting from the provision of tax credits would be more than compensated by the enormous savings under regional subsidies in relation to oil importation and the reduction of the enormous outflow in our foreign exchange to which I have referred.
I believe the points raised by the Manitoba chamber of commerce are worthy of consideration by hon. members. As we know, there is a modest program in being at present through which the government is encouraging the installation of insulation in homes in the provinces of Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia. We do know that many of the other provinces feel it is unfair to be treating those two provinces differently from others in eastern Canada. In my view, the government should give consideration to the interesting suggestion that a tax credit should be available to those who are willing to improve the quality of the insulation of their homes. After all, energy is used by people throughout the nation, and the government might well consider an approach using the incentive to which I have referred. I imagine that many hon. members have received letters from constituents pointing out that they have made additions or improvements affecting the insulation of their homes, and asking why they could not be encouraged to go even further by a provision of tax credits in their favour. For example, I have received a letter in which a constituent said as follows:
With the energy crisis coming closer with each passing day, it behoves all of us to do what we can to conserve what we have. With this end in view I have insulated my whole house with thermal windows and insulation all over the house. As you can well imagine, this is an expensive undertaking and the thought occurred to me that there should be some recognition of this fact by our government via an income tax allowance.
I have written to Mr. Macdonald, the Minister of Finance, and in his reply he gives me two reasons why this cannot be done. Both, to me, appear specious and irrelevant. He says that taxes on all insulation materials have been removed and
Excise Tax Act
that if such an allowance were made it would be of more benefit to the wealthy than to the poorer people.
The writer continued:
A similar letter to Alastair Gillespie has, to date, not brought forth the courtesy of a reply, which is to be expected in view of recent revelations.
I do not know what he is referring to there. But surely it makes sense to take whatever steps we can by way of taxation or otherwise to ensure that less energy is consumed in this country. Success in this respect would mean that whatever problems we encounter in the future will be less serious than would be the case otherwise. But let us go further than the present bill contemplates.
I think it is unfortunate that the minister should have to reveal, as he did yesterday, that though the government has had ample time to consider the matter-they have been aware of the problem for several years, as a matter of fact-his department has somehow given insufficient attention to the fact that the test of weight alone is not the most significant test when seeking to determine how to encourage people to use automobiles capable of using energy economically.
I am pleased, however, that the minister and the department are at least wavering on the position formerly taken, and that the criteria may be altered to include considerations which are more meaningful, for example, the number of miles per gallon a car can travel under Canadian weather conditions. As I have indicated, an excess tax imposed on the basis of weight is not necessarily the most effective means of encouraging energy conservation. My hon. friend from Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) has drawn attention to the fact that by concentrating on vehicle weight it is possible to introduce a distortion into the system of production, which may result in an over-all loss of energy since more would be needed in the production of the cars themselves. That, as I understand it, is the argument put forward by my hon. friend and other colleagues. If stress is laid on the production of light cars which may wear out more quickly than heavier cars, the manufacturer might in the end be required to produce two or three cars for every one of the other vehicles if they were heavier or more reliable.
That is one argument. I should like to advance a second argument. Weight alone, as I have said, is not necessarily the best guide as to which vehicle is the most efficient user of energy. Very often, heavy cars run more efficiently than lighter ones. In any case, the use of the term "weight" can be ambigous because there are four different ways of measuring automobile weight. Mileage per gallon is the best and more equitable. The Department of Finance initially proposed to extend its current excise tax on heavy automobiles to those which are less heavy. Details of this tax were shown originally in the budgetary papers. In general terms, any car weighing in excess of 4,250 pounds in 1976, or 3,500 pounds in 1980, will be subject to a tax in proportion to the excess. The excess tax which was proposed in the budget to encourage fuel conservation was related to the weight of the vehicle.
This move seems likely to encourage the production of lighter cars, but not necessarily cars which use less energy. However, as an official of the finance department put it to me

Excise Tax Act
one day, not only do we need lighter cars but we need more efficient cars. The minister in his remarks yesterday stated the same thing, in effect. As reported at page 2478 of Hansard, he said:
The purpose of the tax is not to raise revenue but rather to encourage Canadians to demand, and the auto industry to produce, lighter and more energy efficient cars.
My point is that we need efficient cars, not necessarily lighter cars, because lighter cars will not necessarily show a better record of energy consumption. I should like to put some figures on the record to demonstrate what I mean. For example, there are four classes of car. According to EPA tests in 1976-and I convert the EPA figures into Imperial gallons- there are four classes of cars which show a mileage reading of 24 m.p.g. They are the Cutlass Oldsmobile, Omega Oldsmo-bile, LeMans Pontiac, and Ventura Pontiac. The curb weight of those vehicles is as follows: the Cutlass Oldsmobile, 4,020 pounds; Omega Oldsmobile, 3,445 pounds; LeMans Pontiac 4,010 pounds; the Ventura Pontiac, 3,440 pounds curb weight. These four cars have six cylinders, yet under the original proposal that we were faced with on May 25 the excise tax on the Cutlass Oldsmobile would have been $500, the Omega Oldsmobile would have had no excise tax, the LeMans Pontiac would have had $300 excise tax, and the Ventura Pontiac no tax.
I could give various mileage rating levels for other cars, including relatively small cars and cars that most of us would consider relatively heavy cars. For example, taking another level, the 21 miles per gallon level, we find that the Matador, of American Motors, weighed in at 3,785 pounds; it has six cylinders and would carry an excise tax of $70. The Seville Cadillac, rated at 21 miles per gallon, has a weight of 4,340 pounds, eight cylinders and an excise tax of $480. The Granada Ford, again at the 21 miles per gallon level, has a weight of 3,540 pounds and eight cylinders, but only an excise tax of $30.
I need not go further with these statistics, Mr. Speaker. I have them for most of the current models which are being sold in Canada. The point I want to make is that as originally conceived the department was wrong in its approach of using the weight test as opposed to the more meaningful miles per gallon test to which I have referred. In short, the original provisions are not equitable. In this last case all automobiles achieved the same energy efficiency, yet are taxed, or would be if the original proposals were to become law, in varying amounts due to difference in weight.
I should emphasize that the tax is calculated by the 1980 case, which is when the ceiling would be 3,500 pounds. As the figures demonstrate, cars achieving an average of only 18 miles per gallon will be taxed about $50, yet a car achieving 23 miles per gallon will be taxed as much as $400. Based on an average travelling distance of 12,000 miles per year, the more heavily taxed car will consume 145 gallons less than that which a less efficient car will use. Let me cite further figures to show another way in which the weight tax is not equitable. I

refer, for example, to the Lincoln-Mercury group of cars which under the EPA fuel economy test are rated at 16 miles per gallon. Their weight is 4,928 pounds. They had an average 1976 list price of $13,014. They will have an average list price by 1979, according to the estimate of the automobile industry, of $19,053. The tax in 1979 would be $840, a 4.4 per cent increase, yet the possible decrease in sales will be from 9 per cent to 22 per cent.
I could cite similar statistics for the Chevelle Chevrolet, Seville Cadillac and Century Buick, but the point I wish to make is that the increase in the price of a car due to the weight tax applied in 1979, if the minister proceeded with his original thinking, would show no corresponding increase in fuel economy. The Seville Cadillac, with 21 miles per gallon, would increase in price by 1.9 per cent; the Delta 88, with 18 miles per gallon, by 6 per cent; and the Thunderbird, with 16 miles per gallon, by 3.9 per cent-the Thunderbird being the statistic that I specifically read into the record.
Perhaps the most blatant example of how weight is not indicative of fuel economy is to compare the Renault 5 to the Peugeot 504 diesel. Although neither could possibly be taxed, this illustrates the point well. Both cars are in the top ten when rated by efficiency. The Renault achieves 39 miles per gallon, and the Peugeot 36. The Renault has a curb weight of 1,835 pounds, yet the Peugeot is 3,045 pounds. Using weight as the single factor to predict efficiency is not accurate. As my first set of figures show, the number of cylinders plays a role. So does the size of the engine and the type of transmission used, whether manual or automatic. Although weight may have more effect on the efficiency of an automobile than any other factor, it is still not the best indicator of fuel economy. The EPA mileage figures are the best indicators, as I have said.
I have cited those figures, Mr. Speaker, because I believe it is unfortunate that the minister is not in a position today to give us his new approach. He has simply said that he is holding back, that at a subsequent time the government is going to alter its approach. If we believe sincerely that this measure was right in its intent to try to conserve energy in this country, the fact is that we are stalling. Once again the government is in a dither. It does not know which way to go, and we, the Canadian public, are being asked simply to stand still and not-I emphasize "not"-press for needed tax changes to ensure less energy consumption by automobiles.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I hope that in addition to giving us his further thoughts as to what type of approach he intends to bring in at a later date, the minister will also reply to the question why the government does not reverse its tactic. Why is it only suitable to increase excise tax on certain vehicles and not remove it on vehicles which the government thinks are the most efficient when it comes to mileage? Would it not make more sense to identify the cars that are least energy-consuming, and lower the tax on those cars so that people, especially those in lower income brackets who wish to buy this sort of car, can do so at lower cost than is the case today?

Although the government says it is not looking for additional revenue, its response is not to reduce excise tax to enable more efficient vehicles to be purchased by people, especially in the lower income brackets. The government proposes to increase the tax on other vehicles. With all due respect, I suggest that this will not have the desired effect which the department thinks it will have. Those who wish to buy big cars, by whatever test they like to choose, are probably going to continue to buy them despite relatively high tax, while the government gives no encouragement at all to persons of lower income to buy the relatively efficient cars, encouragement which a reduction in the excise tax on such vehicles would give.
I would also stress that the effect of the weight tax could be severe. General Motors has announced that starting with their 1977 line, all their full-sized cars will be eliminated. Ford is pursuing a longer-range project which aims to increase the fuel economy of their automobiles. Introduction of a weight tax for 1977 model cars will leave Ford at a competitive disadvantage. All of their new small cars will not be introduced until the introduction of the 1978 models in the fall of 1977. The industry is preparing for 1980 fuel economy measures. Throwing another measure, weight, into the works could undermine the industry's research. I have mentioned this because the minister indicated that they have drawn back, but he has also stated they are awaiting the alternative approach they are going to finally bring in as they review with industry and other officials the proper course to follow in this field.
The weight tax is anticipated to net the government, as it was originally estimated, $35 million. This figure implies that the government has estimated the effect that the tax will have. Indeed, it has not. The figure, rather, is ball-park figure, the average of a tax with no effect on the market and the average earning of a tax with considerable effect. Similarly, the estimated revenue of $7 million from the excise tax on automobile air-conditioners only represents the mean of an upper and lower estimate of $10 million and $5 million. Thus, the statisticians do not know whether the tax will result in the sale of 100,000 air-conditioners or half that many. One must wonder whether, considering the apparent lack of precision in determining the effect, the government is merely instituting another money winner or is really serious about energy conservation. During our committee of the whole review of this bill, I hope the minister will be in a position to give us some estimate as to what he anticipates will be the revenue from the various taxes we have before us in Bill C-21.
Probably the best indicator for the effect the tax will have is the price elasticity given by the industry. In the automotive industry a 1 per cent increase in the price of a car can result in a 2 per cent to a 5 per cent drop in vehicle demand. It is not clear whether this relationship is applicable to individual autos. For instance, rather than having sales of all taxed cars drop by their assigned percentage points, we might find that everyone affected by the tax might buy a less expensive car. Thus, only the most expensive cars would experience a
Excise Tax Act
decrease in sales. I would emphasize, again, that while these cars may be expensive, they may also be relatively efficient energy burners. Another factor is that the sale of more expensive luxury cars tends to be less sensitive to price changes.
In short, before leaving this discussion of weights I want to note that four kinds of weight measures are used. The weight measure used by Revenue Canada at the moment is the individual weight of the car including factory-installed options as shipped from the plant, plus 25 pounds, as I understand it, for gasoline. The second is the shipping weight of the car, which is the average weight of the model of the car. The third standard is the curb weight, which is the average weight of a model of car equipped with radio, automatic transmission, power-steering and the usual type of equipment on that car. Weights of mid-sized and large, luxury cars include air-conditioning. The fourth standard is the inertia weight of the car, which is the average weight of a model of car, plus 300 pounds to give the effect of a partially-loaded car with two people and some luggage. It is this weight that the EPA uses to determine the fuel economy and emission control standards generally accepted in the industry. If weight is to be used as the basis for an excise tax, it seems that the inertia weight is the easiest to work with and the one that reflects true driving situations.
I have summarized some of our thoughts concerning the provisions of the bill we will be dealing with shortly in committee of the whole. I hope the minister, in his opening remarks, will expand on what he said yesterday. I believe we have advanced an interesting thought in an attempt to ensure greater energy conservation as far as automobiles are concerned. Unfortunately, the government has fallen short in that it has misconceived its approach by putting too high a stress on weight and has not given proper incentive to people to buy the most efficient energy-consuming cars by lowering the sales tax rather than simply proposing that the excise tax be raised on certain other cars.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That being the case, I would indicate to hon. members that there is no point of order.

Mr. Speaker, I have almost to jar myself into reality when 1 remind myself that we are still debating the budget of last May 25. I realize there has been a lot of water under the bridge, but most of the measures we are now discussing are basically housekeeping measures that should have been taken care of a long time ago.
I cannot understand why it has taken so long to bring these measures forward. Actually, I find some measures in the budget attractive. Measures encouraging us to find ways to preserve our energy resources are commendable. I am also pleased to note the provision in the budget which will allow the handicapped, or at least the parents of handicapped children, to deduct certain expenses from taxable income. I have talked to the minister's parliamentary secretary about that particular measure which has been, I think, the subject of a private member's motion. I was pleased to note that the minister is in agreement with my position on that matter and that there is to be an enlargement of those provisions which will benefit those who must incur the expense of caring for handicapped children. I commend the minister for enlarging those provisions.
The bill before us leads me to observe that most of its provisions are revenue-producing ones and are designed to discourage expenditures; for example, which would increase our consumption of energy. On the other hand, some of the handicapped in this country, unfortunately, must still pay excise tax on certain equipment they use. Not long ago a constituent called me saying that she is forced to use a wheelchair on which the government charges excise tax. Because she needs a wheelchair all the time, she is forced to

buy a good one which will not wear out quickly: You must pay more for high-quality wheelchairs, and therefore more excise tax. She feels that she is being penalized for being a cripple.
We have come to a very sorry state in this country if we must raise revenue from the handicapped to fill the government's coffers. Really, such an excise tax becomes a tax on misfortune. Surely we can find other ways of raising government revenues, ways other than imposing tax on the handicapped. We should not look to them to provide this revenue. I know the minister is not interested in collecting money from such people, but this practice has grown up over the years, probably because of an oversight. I give the minister notice of my intention to ask him about this matter when we consider the bill in committee of the whole.
It is anomalous that doctors who treat such patients are allowed to rush to their aid in motor vehicles and to collect a rebate on the ten-cents per gallon excise tax on the gasoline used. Doctors do not supply the government with excise tax revenue in that regard; unfortunately, their patients must pay the excise tax. It seems to me that there is an imbalance in this area which I know the minister will want to correct.
Further to that, I raise the question of how one goes about establishing the legitimacy of a deduction under this heading. Many of these decisions come under the purview or decisionmaking powers of particular tax officials who must deal with a citizen making a claim for deduction. If the official is experienced, or if he has some insight into the problem, he will look kindly at the request for a deduction. But the handy-dandy guide put out by the Income Tax Department talks about allowances for the blind and people in wheelchairs. I suggest that that is a limited way of looking at it. A strict constructionist in the income tax department would construe that phrase as applying strictly to the blind and people in wheelchairs.
Surely a host of other people suffering from a handicap and who incur extra expenses should be allowed a deduction with regard to the equipment needed for their care. Unfortunately, at present they are subject to the tax. We are asking cripples to establish a case for justifying these deductions. In other words, how far are you to go in asking a cripple to prove that he is a cripple? Any dossier compiled about him is likely to haunt him later in life.
Remember how Senator Eagleson of the United States was haunted later in life because at one time he had taken psychiatric treatment! Surely we need more compassion; we need to give specific instructions to departmental officials to be more compassionate. I am making the case that it is time to inject more heart into our income tax measures as well as into the administration of the Income Tax Act and more heart into the implementation of those measures in order to ameliorate the lot of those unfortunate enough to suffer a handicap. Doctors know who those people are. I suggest that we should not collect revenue in this way from those suffering; we should not impose a tax on misfortune.
January 28, 1977

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank hon. members of the House for the contributions they have made in the difficult area of the Excise Tax Act, and I shall take the opportunity to respond to the points raised last night by the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) and also to some of the several points raised today.
If I may deal with the comments of the hon. member for Edmonton West, he made an observation with regard to the minimum federal limits for the collection of excise tax. The same point was made this morning by the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Whittaker) to do with the $3,000 limit. It was suggested that because of inflation and the passage of time, that level should be raised. I think I should emphasize that the purpose of that levei primarily is to assist small business. It was based on the calculation on the part of the Department of National Revenue as to the least amount it was worth while collecting in revenue. Having said that, I acknowledge at the same time that if the collection of small sums is hardly worth while for the Department of National Revenue, it is, equally, an imposition for small businessmen, and in that sense I think the comment made by the hon. gentlemen was an important one. This is a matter falling within the administrative duties of my colleague, the Minister of National Revenue (Miss Begin). I can say to the House that the minister has been giving consideration to the currency or appropriateness of that particular limitation, that this matter is under consideration, and that the minister, when she is in a position to do so, I am sure will be prepared to comment.
The hon. member for Edmonton West referred to extensive correspondence which has flowed between himself, myself and others with regard to a particular kind of insulating panel. In one case, as I recall, the panel was made out of compressed straw. The hon. member made the point that since the panel had insulating qualities, it should be treated as insulating material under the Excise Tax Act and, therefore, tax free. To some degree the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens) raised the same point when he talked about thermal window panes. Both hon. members in their comments put their finger on the difficult borderline of what is essentially a building material and what is essentially a material used for insulating purposes. The position which has been taken in the law is one that is directed purely to insulation such as bats to be fitted into the walls or ceilings of a house. Obviously, these would be tax free.
Excise Tax Act
Others which have a primary building quality to them, or at least in addition to the quality of insulation-and of course every piece of material has to a degree the quality of insulation-also have a structural quality, would be treated as building materials and therefore taxable. In particular cases there will have to be an administrative determination as to what is primarily insulation and what is primarily structural material. This has been a difficult area to define under the Excise Tax Act.
The hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge (Mr. Saltsman) raised a number of questions, one on this bill and one in more general terms with respect to correspondence received by the hon. member for Regina Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin). The first question raised by the hon. member for Waterloo-Cambridge was on automobile air conditioners. If a car with the windows down on a hot day has more drag than if the windows are up, and therefore the air conditioning is on, is it not counter productive in an energy conservation sense? The response that would be furnished by the energy conservation branch of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, I believe, would be that the argument might be valid at highway speeds, although even at highway speeds the standard flowthrough mechanism would have a cooling effect in the car. At less than highway speeds we do not have the same drag problem, and in that sense it is obviously felt by energy conservers that the air conditioner does not have that much advantage for energy conservation.
With regard to the correspondence between the Canadian Council of Rehabilitation Workshops and the Minister of National Revenue, several basic questions arise. First, one of the principles under the Excise Tax Act has been that a manufacturer, for example a manufacturer in a rehabilitation workshop, can become a licensed manufacturer under the Excise Tax Act and in that sense will be exempt from the payment of sales tax on materials that he uses in manufacturing, but in turn would have to collect sales tax when he sells to a subsequent purchaser. The problem, if I understand it, raised in the correspondence arose in a situation where you have rehabilitation workshops which repair articles of furniture, equipment, or other articles. The position taken with regard to repairing artisans is that in providing a service of that kind they are not generally exempt from excise tax under the statute and they are treated as other people in that they have to pay sales tax.
On the question of the certification of institutions, this is obviously a problem of the practical application of some criteria. I should indicate to the House that the decision in this case is made by the Department of National Health and Welfare which, for the purpose of these exemptions, certifies a particular institution. The issue that was raised was whether, in addition to physical disability as one of the causes of an institution being exempted from tax, that provision should also be extended to institutions which provide assistance or opportunities to those who are socially disadvantaged, such as released inmates of penal institutions, rehabilitated addicts, or

January 28, 1977
Excise Tax Act
persons recovering from alcoholic addiction. This is obviously a difficult decision, but the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) has to determine, in accordance with criteria, what is appropriate. I would be quite happy if the organization would like to address comments to my colleague on these criteria, and naturally I will accept the minister's judgment on this point.
The hon. member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Clarke) gave us an interesting approach to the taxation system. He has put himself out as a long time opponent of the income tax system. Apparently he is also an opponent of the excise tax system. His prescription is that the government should return back to the time prior to the 1914-18 war. I think that a lot of us in some respects would be delighted to have the community as a whole return to that distant era.
I would say idyllic.

I see the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) is here, and I think of my own antecedents in Winnipeg, for example. Indeed, in some cases the time prior to 1914 might have been idyllic. On the other hand, social conditions in which many people lived at that time were far from being so.

I would have to say that, much as one might be sympathetic to the vision to the hon. member for Vancouver Quadra about an older and in some sense simpler era, the intervention of the government on the whole has been for human betterment in Canada, so I suppose I would have to disagree with him on that fundamental principle.

I would defer to the hon. gentleman's obvious experience in that regard.
There was no mayonnaise then.

With regard to the more basic proposition as to whether the sales tax should be abolished altogether and replaced by other taxes in the community, it was estimated in connection with the Carter commission and, I believe, in subsequent discussions, that to replace the current revenue for the government from the sales tax would require something like a 25 per cent increase in personal income tax, or conversely a 65 per cent increase in corporate income tax. In that sense one would have to consider whether this is really desirable. It would become an outward and evident tax, but

also become a very heavy one for individuals to bear, particularly those in certain income categories.
One of the advantages of the sales tax is that the person who uses an item and bears the tax in some cases is in a position to pass it on, and to that extent it is related to the use of a foreign article rather than imposing the cost on the community as a whole.
The hon. member for Okanagan Boundary raised the question of solar heat and asked about the tax on wood stoves. I think there is an argument not just for abolition of the tax on wood stoves but also on other kinds of heating devices which might burn vegetable material. I think his observation in this regard is in the form of a representation which I am prepared to discuss with my colleague with regard to the appropriateness of stimulating a greater use of those energy materials in addition to solar heat and wind generated energy.
Finally, before I deal with the extensive presentation of the hon. member for York-Simcoe with regard to automobiles, I wish to deal with the matter raised by the hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen) with regard to wheelchairs. I am advised that on wheelchairs as such there is no tax, but there may indeed be a problem of definition. Perhaps the hon. member and I could talk about the particular item to which he was referring because it may well be that it is not classified under this particular area, in which case I would be glad to be given further information and to consider it. On wheelchairs as such I acknowledge the thrust of the hon. gentleman's argument that this is not the kind of assistance to a handicapped person which should be subject to extra taxation.
With regard to the argument about the changes in energy conservation measures, there was indeed a parallel between the thinking of the hon. member for York-Simcoe and that of the government on the use of automobile fuel and the possible changes in the taxation system to try to encourage a more efficient use. I have to go back again to the purpose of the change in midsummer as a result of the May 25 budget. The budget proposals really did have the effect of compelling two of the major manufacturers in Canada to come forward and indicate that they were not on the timetable required to handle the weight tax, that they were not trying to solve the energy conservation problem by reducing weights, but that they had a more efficacious method of doing so, and therefore they thought that they should be left with some room within the next year to try to find some other means. One of the major Canadian manufacturers has indeed gone the lower weight route, and that manufacturer will have had the benefit of the lower tax rate.
Others in the group have not, but they are trying to arrive at the same end by different means, and it was on that basis that it can be said that the May 25 budget was effective in putting the pressure on to encourage a greater effort on the part of the automobile industry to come up with a proposal of alternative means of saving energy in automobile locomotion which the government can accept, and therefore by that means we have
January 28, 1977

been effective in stimulating the industry to bring about a faster timetable than would have been the case with an alternative proposition. I just emphasize again that there is a quality of probation in these particular changes and, as I indicated to the industry, we will be prepared to hold off for a year. Unless there can be satisfactory evidence that we are indeed moving to a good alternative formula, then the weight tax will be back again in a form like that in which it was initially introduced.
It is not a question of the government not being able to make up its mind. The government has made up its mind on the weight tax. The weight tax has really compelled the other two firms to come to terms with the measures they propose to take in order to reduce energy consumption.
I think that deals with the main principles of many of the points which have been raised, but there may be additional questions, particularly when the officials get down to the floor, so I will close by thanking hon. members for their contribution and by indicating that I am prepared to entertain further questions as we go through the bill clause by clause.

various approaches which can be taken, the weight test, efficiency tests, and the miles per gallon type of test?

Mr. Chairman, it is the answer I have just given. It has a cost in terms of the lost revenue. It seems reasonable to recover that revenue.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister why he indicated yesterday that essentially it was not revenue production they were seeking but energy conservation. Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman is confusing two things. The comment I made was with regard to the additional taxation that would be raised by the weight tax. In basic terms what I have just referred to in revenue loss is a general excise tax that is available. If we are

successful in our objectives and people move to lighter cars, then there will still be a substantial amount to be collected by the 12 per cent excise tax on automobiles. Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister for some clarification in regard to air conditioners. Would the minister confirm that air conditioners installed in those vehicles do not require payment of the $100 excise tax?
Yes, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, this constituent informs me that the department says because he does not hold a sales tax licence he has to pay this tax upon importation of the product. Mack Truck, International Harvester, and the Ford Motor Company import the same item from the same company and they do not pay tax. As I understand the situation, Mr. Chairman, if he were a licensed dealer he would be exempt from payment of the tax. Where he is an unlicensed dealer, or a licensed manufacturer not having an excise tax licence, if he sells a vehicle without an air conditioner, under exempt conditions he may then claim a refund of the excise tax which he has paid.

Mr. Chairman, I want to ask myself why this man has not applied for a licence to become a licensed dealer. If his business is so considerable, one would have thought this the logical step. Of course I cannot comment on the situation, but that seems the obvious route for him.

He is not then eligible for a wholesaler's licence.

Just to correct the hon. member, Mr. Chairman, the average refund is within 30 days.

Just to correct the minister, I will lay him what I have in my pocket against what he has in his that it is not 30 days. I will bring a lot of people who will show it is not 30 days. I know personally.
The hon. member is very confident, Mr. Chairman, but I intend to rely on National Revenue.

Just to be clear, the obvious goal in revenue terms is zero. Of course there is a general sales tax beneath that on all automobiles. I would require to be convinced that the hon. member's basic proposition is accurate. I am not sure that heavy means long life, particularly in eastern Canada where, among other things, salt is a serious fact of life.

I am not sure of that either. That is why I asked the question whether the government had done any research in that vein. I will presume it has not.
I would like now to ask about a slightly different topic, the tax on air conditioners. Why did the government find it necessary, when the minister announced on May 25 the $100 tax on air conditioning systems for automobiles, to make that retroactive? In other words, why wasn't the sanctity of a contract that had been entered into a month or more before May 25 respected, and those people allowed to have the transaction completed without the interference of the government?

Mr. Chairman, it has been the general practice that, where a change of this kind has occurred, it should be effective as of budget night. One can think of a range of possible options sooner or later from the date of budget night, but the final conclusion, from experience over time, is that from an administrative standpoint and probably fairness standpoint this is the most reasonable way to handle it. One of the difficulties, of course, is that it would give a distinct advantage to those manufacturers who have a substantial inventory on hand as of budget night, for example.

That explanation may be all right for those who were contemplating a purchase, but for those who had purchased in good faith under an existing contract there is nothing in budget history to imply that existing contracts should not be honoured. However, the minister has given me an answer, and I thank him for that.
It is my understanding that the minister in his closing remarks on second reading made some reference to my earlier remarks which he did not seem to understand. They concerned the imposition of a sales tax and the personal income tax.
I am not sure where I saw the term used, but in the minister's budget remarks he referred to the sales or consumption tax. I cannot find that at the moment. If it were necessary, I am sure I could dig it up. In any event the reference was made to a consumption or sales tax, implying that the government sees them as being the same.
The purpose of my remarks is not to say that all taxes are bad. I am simply remarking that the government seems to have a great inconsistency in that it uses this kind of a hidden tax, the personal income tax, and many other kinds of taxes. However, each kind of tax comes from the same taxpayer. Each kind of tax requires a substantial bureaucracy here in
