Ottawa to enforce and collect it. Each kind of tax requires a similar bureaucracy in the private sector. In fact every business is required to make the calculation, whether it be a corporate income tax, personal income tax of the individual proprietors, or sales tax returns for the excise tax. All of these taxes go on and on.
The thrust of my remarks was that the government should spend more time exploring ways to ease the burden on the taxpayer so that he is better able to judge where he is being taxed, where the burden of tax lies in his daily life, and to simplify the burden from the point of view of reducing the bureaucracy required on the part of the government, and thereby reducing the size of the bureaucracy that is required in business.
The government seems to forget, in all its dealings in the various tax fields, that there is ultimately only one source of tax revenue, and that is the ordinary taxpayer. The taxpayer deserves far more consideration from this government than he is getting. I am thinking of the proliferation of the demands made upon him and the disregard shown for the individual, whether he be a labourer, a salaried person or a businessman. That was the essence of my criticism of the tax systems. It is not that I criticize them per se. Of course the government needs its revenue. But in my view the government ought to give greater consideration to the source of this revenue, to the nature of its revenue base.

Perhaps I could return to the line of questioning I was putting to the minister. It turned on the amount of revenue the government expects to get from the new taxes which are before us. As I understand it, the minister told us there would be some $7 million on account of the tax on air conditioners, and between $5 million and $10 million on account of the automobile weight tax. This represents a combined increase of some $12 million to $17 million flowing into the treasury.
Bearing in mind the minister's candid statement that the purpose of the new tax was not to raise revenue but rather to encourage Canadians to demand, and the auto industry to produce, lighter and more energy efficient cars, my question is this: why would the minister not consider, in addition to imposing this new tax, reducing taxation on lighter cars by a like amount? He tells us he expects to get between $5 million and $10 million in extra taxes. Would he not think it appropriate to lower taxes on the lighter cars, presumably on the more energy-efficient cars to which he referred, by a comparable amount?

As I indicated earlier, a basic amount flows into revenues from existing automobile taxation. I suppose there might be a marginal rate change but I am not certain that this would be practical from an administrative standpoint. We have to recognize with regard to the excise tax generally that automobiles are a source of revenue, and we expect they will continue to be so.
(Mr. Clarke.]

Would the minister at least go thus far: would he, between now and the next budget, give consideration to lowering the tax on the more efficient cars within the parameters of the revenue to which reference has been made?
Some of the conservationists might take exception to that and argue that by making a further tax cut I would be encouraging the acquisition of cars, but I will look into that suggestion.

I am pleased to get that assurance from the hon. gentleman. If he is belaboured by the conservationists I hope he will remind them that the light, energy efficient car to which I am referring is very greatly needed by most Canadians for commuting to work and for other necessary aspects of their livelihood. In short, it is an essential in spite of what some conservationists might attempt to tell the minister.

Clause agreed to.
On clause 7.

Clause 7 includes the energy conservation equipment item. Can the minister tell us whether any studies have been carried out to show how practical are some of these energy conservation devices to which the clause refers? We know, for example, about the possibilities of solar energy generation, wind generators and so on. Surely the department, or a related agency, must have carried out studies as to how practical it is to encourage people to go in for these alternative ways of heating. If so, what has been the result of such a study?

There have obviously been a variety of advances in this field. The insulation materials are all of longstanding application and the effectiveness of the existing materials has been well proven. Heat pumps, for example, do not represent a particularly esoteric technology. On the other hand, there is a rapidly expanding field of technology related to the use of solar energy. The wind generator has been known for a long time, of course, even if really effective means of exploiting that source of power has not been discovered. But to the extent that there is new technology involved here, or the improvement of existing technology, the goal is to encourage the development of better and more efficient devices, and we think it worth while to pursue this course.
The basic question the hon. member raises is, of course, an important one. There are long steps yet to be taken in technology, and this is why we are bound to move cautiously when conservationists tell us that we should not be using fossil or nuclear fuels. We think more favourable tax terms would assist in the technological development which is necessary.

I do not think anyone would disagree with the minister when he says people who go in for these less conventional energy sources should be encouraged. I was wondering, though, whether he is giving any consideration to dealing with one of the basic problems, that is, energy storage. Has he, for instance, made any overtures to the power companies in the
January 28, 1977

various provinces to see whether they would agree to buy power which might be generated by the wind or by solar rays? As I understand it, one direct approach would be an arrangement under which power generated by a wind generator could be fed into the system of a power company and drawn back as needed over subsequent days or months. This would be a very practical approach if it could be worked out. At the present time expensive storage battery facilities are required whenever privately generated power needs to be held for future consumption.

I would be glad to pass on the hon. member's comments to my colleague, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. In preparing the tax bill the department did not have that kind of conservation in mind. It is an interesting thought.

I have one question for the minister. It arises from clause 7. Reference is made, on page eight, to thermal insulation materials designed exclusively for insulation purposes, storm doors and storm windows for buildings. Would thermopane used in construction or reconstruction fall into that category, or could you make it fall into that category?
I am advised it does fall into that category.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
that Bill C-214, to register lobbyists, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.
He said: Mr. Speaker, lobbying has not been a subject of great concern to Canadians, in contrast to the attention given to it by legislatures, journalists, and political scientists in the United States. Because of the profound differences between our systems of government, I doubt that Canadian lobbyists will ever achieve the important and sometimes controversial status that they now have there. Nevertheless, the direction in which our parliamentary system should be evolving-toward a more open government with a more influential House of Commons-leads me to believe that we should begin now to establish a framework for the operation of lobbyists before any serious problems develop.
First, Mr. Speaker, what is a lobbyist? I think of a lobbyist as someone who seeks, by means of contact with persons of power or influence, to have a significant effect on executive or legislative actions to be taken by the government of Canada. Lobbyists may act directly for themselves, or on behalf of organizations which hire professionals to make their case. Lobbyists are, in short, special interest and pressure group publicists or their representatives.
Lobbying has had, especially in the United States, a pejorative connotation-and I think that is rather unfortunate-but it is an important and absolutely necessary part of democratic government. Lobbyists are able to provide legislators with feedback on the actual operation of government programs in the field. There is, as we all know, many a slip between bureaucratic theory, on the one hand, and field experience, on the other hand. The sooner governments and all of us find out about that, the better our programs might be understood.
Lobbyists also provide background information of a more general nature about action that is under consideration. We are all used to dealing with "pressure" from associations which are to be affected by legislation, but in fact much of this pressure is informed argument which is sometimes difficult to refute. It is also preferable on many occasions to deal with a carefully prepared presentation by a spokesman for a scattered interest group rather than to deal with the unorganized and incomplete ideas of a large number of individuals. Finally, I put it to you, Sir, that lobbyists are useful when we want to try out ideas, as we soon find out if they have any merit or whether those ideas are simply naive. All these functions

January 28, 1977
Lobbying
performed by lobbyists are indispensable to the reflective as well as the responsive politician.
Naturally, pressure can take illegitimate and illegal forms and have unfortunate consequences, and these dangers bring me to suggest registration of lobbyists. There is, of course, the possibility of bribery, blackmail or other questionable practices. It is the hope that contacts, which must be made with the knowledge of anyone who cares to examine a register, would be less likely to have a shady dimension. There is an even greater danger that if pressure is carried on secretively or unobstrusively, all sides of a debate will not be heard and legitimate points of view or bodies of information will be excluded until a stage in the debate when decisions have been irrevocably taken. At the present time, Mr. Speaker, that seems to be when a bill has been introduced in the House of Commons.
Or there may simply be a suspicion that pressure behind the scenes is by that very fact illegitimate pressure, and the resulting policies might not obtain the support they merit because people feel that certain groups or types of groups have had an unhealthy impact. Then there is the other side of the coin. If we have that knowledge and know that all arguments have been equally heard, I think there would be a tendency for there to be a reconciliation of the diversity of groups which are affected by decisions that might be taken.
In short, the purpose of the bill is to ensure that lobbying, as much as possible, is conducted in the open so that people can see who is trying to influence what, and if necessary respond. Where lobbying is done with the knowledge of everyone concerned, there is a better chance that it will be done openly and that improper practices will have a smaller chance of survival or success. The process of decision making should become more educational and the results more acceptable.
My bill would take the first step toward publicizing lobbying activities in Canada, though I have to say at the outset, Mr. Speaker, that it is a small step indeed. It defines lobbying, to paraphrase, as the actions of any person or any group attempting to influence the course of either legislative or executive action. It establishes a register of lobbyists to be administered jointly by the Clerks of the two Chambers. Lobbyists must set down their names, the person or group on whose behalf they are acting, and the duration of any contact. This information must be supplied before any contacts are made, supplemented with any new information applicable and submitted afresh at the beginning of every year. I have included penalties for non-compliance of up to $5,000 per month and prohibition from lobbying for two years, to show that the register which is set forth in the bill is intended to be taken seriously.
I would not deny that this is little more than a beginning which leaves a good many questions unanswered, and many of these questions have been suggested by people writing to me from all across the country about the bill. A bill discussed in the United States House of Representatives on this subject last year ran to 39 pages, and this matter is already the subject of extensive legislation there.

If I might indicate some of the unanswered questions, I put them as examples and there are probably more. Do we want to monitor the type of lobbying activity as well as the existence of the activity? How do we classify officials of companies or organizations who come to Ottawa only briefly to meet officials or legislators? Does it matter who instigates discussions between lobbyists and officials? Should we consider contact with a minister's or member's staff as lobbying? When does assistance to our constituents become activity on behalf of, or in response to, a lobbyist?
The intention is that those whose principal function is to lobby on behalf of others be regulated, not those whose occupation is administrative or whatever, but who occasionally must defend their interest by contact with politicians or officials. This is not an easy distinction to make, and I would welcome the views of others on the proper bounds for restrictions, and would like to see serious consideration by a committee of this House of the whole question.
The question that will occur to many members may be, why should it be necessary to contemplate action when we have survived without it for over a century? As I suggested earlier, I believe we are moving in a number of ways, or at least we should be moving, toward more open government. This will create both opportunities and dangers. To date lobbyists have dealt principally through public service channels, and in theory at least these contacts have a minimum of danger because the interests and motivations of those concerned are clearly defined and established within an administrative framework. If legislators become more prominent in policy formation, I believe lobbying activity will increase and should be open, because in the political process motivations and interests are not so easily defined or traced.
I believe that the role of legislators will change for a variety of reasons. First, it appears to me that people have become increasingly demanding of their members of parliament, and they will perhaps become more demanding after they watch us on TV. They will, I believe, expect us to be more critical and more creative. I think too that members are increasingly equipped to meet this challenge and are intent on doing so.
Secondly, I believe that within the next few years, and it is my hope, we will have a freedom of information bill which will enable members of this Chamber to participate in the discussion of policy options prepared by the public service. Perhaps we will need a change of government before that degree of open policy debate is obtained, but it is coming, and the increased insight and opportunities we will have will invite contacts from those who now restrict themselves to permanent officials.
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Do not be too subjective, I would suggest to hon. members.
Thirdly, and particularly if this party transfers to the other side of the Chamber, which would seem likely, our committees
January 28, 1977

will be given the power and the staff to undertake investigative and creative functions on behalf of the House. Again, as the number of participants in the debate on national priorities increases, the presence of lobbyists will become more pervasive. I hope too that we can make private members' hour more conclusive and, if we do, the lobbyists will be after us to champion their views, or oppose someone else's.
Fourth, to be realistic about the results of any change in government which may take place there would be more pressure group activity, particularly because many policies which are non unchallengeable as part of the dominant mythology would be subject to review and debate on any policy, and any policy shift invites lobby contacts.
Finally, I hope lobbying is conducted more openly in the future because of a trend in respect of pressure groups which has already developed in our society. Some hon. members may have seen the text of a speech delivered June 6 by the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), the former leader of our party. He said at that time:
We are becoming a society of well-organized groups representing a particular interest or point of view. The number of groups organized to put on pressure have become legion. This is increasing the tension and distrust in our society; and it is increasing the difficulty of reaching a consensus as a basis for government in a country where consensus has always been difficult to achieve anyway. People not only see their own particular interest but have an organization to promote it. This has already led to a lot of governmental floundering and could well make government initiatives very difficult to take; and further increase the sense of frustration among citizens.
These special interest organizations are more attractive to join and support than political parties because political parties are not designed to serve (although they sometimes do) particular interests. To get elected they have to appear at least to be serving the interest of the country generally, rather than some particular interest or cause. So to a growing number of Canadians, political parties seem to be less attractive in serving their cause then does that particular organization designed specifically to serve their cause.
He concluded in this way:
This is leading to a hardening and strengthening of the pushing of particular interests and attitudes which emphasize division and conflict and a weakening of the only institutions we had which encouraged some regard for the common welfare and some recognition of the other fellow's point of view, especially national political parties.
It is a rather wise statement about what is happening in our society today.
Let me conclude by saying I hope the registration of all lobbying groups or individuals will illustrate to Canadians the intricacies of group accommodation and the need to pursue a consensus which is unlikely to fulfil all the aspirations of any particular group. I hope openness will encourage realistic expectations among our electors as well as continued aboveboard dealing between pressure groups and administrators and politicians.
Lobbyists also provide background information of a more general nature about action that is under consideration. We are used to dealing with pressure from associations, associations which are affected by legislation. I think that in the course of our dealings with this pressure the hon. member for Halifax spoke of, with the development of associations and groups within society, each of us as members of parliament feel there must be some response. When that activity, which
Lobbying
we regard as legitimate in the course of interaction which must occur between the private and public sectors, reaches the proportions it has, then there is nothing wrong and nothing inhibiting in having those who would engage legitimately in that activity register their interests and their extent, and to keep that registration fresh with the Clerks of both Houses of this parliament.
It is in that spirit, a spirit that I hope this House will agree is in accordance with a movement toward openness in government, which at least from our point and I hope from the other side will be coming, that I ask this House to consider this bill. I ask the House to send it to committee at least for study. I said during the course of my speech that I did not regard it as the last word, by any means, but this is the first word in respect of a problem and concern of many people.
A jurist once said that not only must things be correct and proper, they must appear to be correct and proper. I think this bill will go a long way to helping not only the substance but the appearance of the substance in regard to a legitimate public activity.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to speak on the bill presented by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker). The subject of registering lobbyists is something that has long interested me. I am certain the hon. member will appreciate that I too have a bill on lobbying, Bill C-248, but it looks as though, according to the pecking order in getting bills before the House, that the hon. member is much more successful than I.
The explanatory note to my bill reads:
The purpose of this bill is to require the identification of lobbyists, persons who, in the interest of others, seek to influence Senators or Members of the House of Commons to vote or use influence for, or against, a matter which may come before parliament. Nothing in the bill restricts lobbying, paid or otherwise, or in any way interferes with the right of the public to make representations to Members of the Senate and of the House of Commons. Similar legislation in effect in the United States requires that lobbyists register with the Clerk of the Legislature and secure an identification card from the said Clerk.
I note that the explanatory note to the hon. member's bill reads:
This bill provides for the registration of lobbyists, and a declaration by them stating in whose interest they are working. It imposes a fine and disqualification from lobbying for those convicted of evading these provisions.
The two bills have much in common. I am sure hon. members appreciate that bills to do with lobbying have been dealt with by other jurisdictions, but that this subject has not been seriously dealt with in this country.
I presume the intention of this bill is to make the public aware and provide for public scrutiny of the individuals and organizations that hope to influence government policy and legislation. This would also allow the civil service, with whom many lobbyists deal, to know whom they were really talking to and why.

January 28, 1977
Lobbying
This proposal certainly has its merits. Lobbying can be defined as the deliberate organization and application of effort to influence public policy, generally for the benefit of some specific person or group. Consequently if this bill came into force, any person or persons attempting to affect some legislative change, extract some favour or influence policy, could be identified through public disclosure. This would also allow the public to gauge lobbyists, success by the subsequent rejection or acceptance of their proposals by the government.
However, the basis of this bill seems to be founded on the premise that interest groups and the government and civil service are in adversary roles. I am not at all convinced that this is the case. In a recent study concerning pressure groups and government, David Kwavnick discovered that there are many benefits to be had from the co-operation of interest groups and government officials. Certainly it is apparent that cabinet members frequently request information from organizations that fall under their jurisdictions. The meetings between the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) and the President of the Canadian Labour Congress are one such example. I think it is fair to say that Canadian politicians are willing to consult with specific interest groups. I might also add that this could be extended to the civil service. As Kwavnick points out, "the popular notion of government officials having continually to fend-off badgering, bullying, and bribing lobbyists is a long way from the truth."
Robert Presthus has said, regarding lobbyists, that the rise to prominence of standing committees has "made interest group directors more aware of members of parliament." However, Mr. Presthus contends, with some justification, that this awareness is diluted by lobbyists concern with cabinet members and senior civil servants. A statistical survey shows that only 15 per cent of lobbyists focussed their attention on members of Parliament, while 40 per cent concentrated on cabinet ministers and 26 per cent on the public service. Clearly backbenchers have low priority. Conversely, of federal and provincial members of parliament questioned, only 18 per cent placed any importance on lobbyists as representatives of community interest.
It is to this point, civil service interaction with lobbyists, that I would like to address my comments. According to Walter Lee, who could be described as the lobbyists' lobbyist, "policy is nearly always made by the civil service." Mr. Lee goes on to say that the only effective way to influence proposed legislation is to "anticipate it well in advance." He also contends that a lobbyist working through carefully selected contacts in the civil service can make his case.
The Toronto Star, of June 21, 1975, reported that business and industry are almost eager to help with and perhaps influence the planning and policies of the civil service. The Star goes on to say that it is with this sub-cabinet group that lobbyists have their greatest influence. Certainly a substantial percentage of lobbyists agree, according to Robert Presthus. Mr. Speaker, I might also point out that various organizations campaign for a president or chairman who is familiar with government routine and is known in government circles-for

example, the case of Mr. Simon Reisman, ex-deputy minister of finance who has become a "consultant".
As we all know, many large associations and organizations have taken offices in Ottawa for the express purpose of lobbying. The biggest of these, the Canadian Manufacturers Association, the Canadian Labour Congress, and the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, present briefs and publicize their views before each federal budget. They also maintain year-round contacts with civil servants who may be working on legislation that effects them.
The survival of any organization that claims to represent its members effectively depends on its ability to persuade the power holders to recognize them as a legitimate bargaining agent. Interest groups have developed links with the existing political and social structure to ensure the protection of their interests and also to keep open direct lines to the government.
It is my contention that it is well and good to demand that lobbyists register. It would act as a point of clarification. However, what effect would it have on the civil service?
A fairly substantial school of opinion suggests that a great deal of lobbying is concentrated on senior civil servants. Would a member of an interest group have to register if he were to talk with a government official? What about the non-lobbying co-operation that now exists between such departments as Supply and Services and private enterprise? When a pencil supplier places a bid with Supply and Services would he have to register as a lobbyist? After all, any initiative he might show in encouraging Supply and Services to award him the contract could be interpreted as lobbying.
I received a letter from the executive director of the Canadian Trucking Association with regard to this particular issue. The letter, dated November 7, 1974, was addressed to me, signed by A. K. Maclaren as executive director, and originated, according to the letterhead, apparently from 130 Albert Street, Suite 300, Ottawa. He allowed that to alleviate some concerns and to satisfy curiosity it might not be a bad idea to require people who wished to make representations to government to register. However, he also supposed that 95 per cent of all representations were made off Parliament Hill. He questioned the efficacy of restricting lobbying controls only to Parliament Hill, and wondered if a chat between a constituent and his member of parliament that touched on some current legislative matter could be construed as lobbying.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I think that my hon. colleague has brought an important issue to our attention. Certainly the public has the right to know who is working behind the scenes, for whom he may be working, why he is doing so and, perhaps most important, for how much. In many cases members of this House would benefit from this information as well as the people of Canada. Free and easy access to this type of information would also mean that any questionable activity would quickly come to light, and consequently it is likely it would cease.
Despite the fine efforts of the hon. member to control and publicize this practice, I must state that there are many

questions that remain untouched. How will registering affect the interaction of civil servants and lobbyists? And how could this interaction be monitored, if it were theoretically controlled? I might add, Mr. Speaker, that while I have used the term "civil servant" freely here today, I appreciate that not all officials are subject to lobbyist pressure, and I have not intended to impugn the characters of our civil servants in any way.
I must commend the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton, but I must also call for further study of this complicated and complex issue.

Mr. Speaker, like the hon. member who has just taken his seat, I should like to see this bill or its subject matter referred to a committee, so that this whole question can be aired and studied in depth. I believe that one way to present the idea I want to place before the House is to tell a story about something which happened in this place so long ago that only one other member of this House was here at the time, and he is enjoying the sun in the Caribbean. Therefore I am not talking about anybody who is here today.
There was a certain government bill which had been presented and which I happened to favour, but which drew the opposition of the life insurance companies of this country. The bill got second reading-after all the government had a good majority and it saw to it that the bill was given second reading-and went to a standing committee. By the time the bill got to that committee we found ourselves faced with a powerful lobby from the insurance companies of Canada. They saw all of us who were members of the committee in our offices, and they made representations to the committee.
My memory of the experience is that of one of the most vigorous lobbies I have known. We had a tough time in the committee. After all, the pressure had been put on, and for a while it looked as if the government bill might actually be defeated in the standing committee. There were two or three members on the government side who had not been attending the committee who were rounded up by a Liberal who had some progressive ideas, and when the vote came, we won. The bill passed in the committee; we defeated the lobby.
The session went on but the bill was never called for third reading. I went to one of my friends in the Liberal cabinet of that day and asked him, "What happened? We defeated the lobby, we passed the bill. How come it has not been brought back for third reading?" He said, "Stanley, you must realize that one of those insurance fellows, one of the men at the top, got to the right cabinet minister". It was not even the minister in whose name the bill was before us but the "right cabinet minister", and that ended that.
If the point of that story is not obvious, I suppose I can spell it out. The lobbying that is effective, or that counts around this place, is not the lobbying of individual members of the House
Lobbying
of Commons but the lobbying of the government itself, the lobbying of cabinet ministers.
I agree with the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson) that this matter should be studied. I join him in congratulating the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) for bringing it before us.
I note that in his opening remarks the sponsor made a point which occurred to me, namely, that our situation is quite different from the situation in Washington. There the effects of lobbying on individual Congressmen can have much greater results than the lobbying of individuals here because they have more control of the purse strings than we do. Therefore I say that this question of registering lobbyists may not have as important a bearing here as it has in Washington. It may not be the most important cog in the regime that my friend would like to see established.
I see this as a piece of legislation that goes along with legislation respecting the freedom of information and legislation respecting conflict of interest, and I say to my friend, and perhaps he would even agree with me, that those other two things are more important than the registration of lobbyists.
Reference has just been made to the Canadian Labour Congress, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Public Service Alliance of Canada, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, and so on. They all have permanent offices here, and the persons who are officers of those bodies, or who are employed by them, lobby. Are they lobbyists within the meaning of this bill? They would say they are not paid for lobbying, they are paid to do the work of their organizations. But, like my friend who has just spoken, I see nothing wrong with those organizations, particularly the ones I named, because they are out in the open making their case.
What concerns me is the kind of lobbying that goes on in ministers' offices behind closed doors. I think that, important as it is to deal with this question of lobbying, completely open government-to use my friend's phrase-is necessary, and in order to achieve that we must have freedom of information which goes all the way-and I do not see any sign of it yet- and we must also have a clearer position with respect to conflict of interest. We have to know what are the financial interests of cabinet ministers, senators, members of parliament, and senior public servants, and if we had better legislation in those areas we would move closer to an open kind of government and the honest decisions that my friend wants.
I hope that the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton does not feel that I am damning his bill with faint praise. I think it is an important subject which should be thoroughly studied, but what I am most grateful for is the opportunity we are given to insist on the importance of these other things as well, namely, freedom of information and clear legislation with respect to conflict of interest. Having said these things, and having given them what I think is their relative importance, I would like to see either this bill or its subject matter referred to a committee so that this important issue can be thoroughly studied.

January 28, 1977
Lobbying

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) on his very important bill and his impressive arguments. Personally I think it is a most interesting bill, but I wonder if it is possible ever to get consensus on what is a lobbyist. As the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson) asked, are these various organizations from labour and manufacturers' associations, to the million people espousing the right to live, lobbyists? And should they all be registered? I am indeed extremely ambivalent about lobbyists because I believe that some are sincere and concerned and do not even require registration, while those who are paid lobbyists often are not sincere in what they are doing; they simply want to make their money and run to the next assignment.
I would have many questions to ask if this bill went to committee. I believe that good private members' bills should not be talked out, yet here I am talking about this bill and I have some important things I want to say with regard to the reference of the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore to the public service. I am sure that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has seen, in his long experience, the virtues and dangers of lobbyists in our society. It is said that pressure groups are essential to good government. I fear, however, the pressure point that is most often used is key senior people in the public service-a point illustrated by the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore when he said that 26 per cent of the lobbying is on the public service. I suspect that the figure is much higher, and that is why I did want to speak on this subject today. I believe that the most dangerous pressure of special interest groups may be on senior public servants who themselves want to run this country. We have ample evidence of this in my area certainly.
It is with great fear that I see what is happening to this country. There are senior public servants who resent interference from the elected representatives. At times I feel that possibly a few senior key civil servants may well be in collusion with the lobbyists. They are certainly out to control the country through their own offices. They want the elected representatives to take the blame, the flak. They do not want to take the responsibility for actions in the public arena. We are taking the blame for many things that are created by key civil servants who, I am sure, have been influenced by back room lobbying. We will not ever get those people to register.
I think of Bill C-58. We saw Reader's Digest out in the open, but we did not see that great multinational corporation which is now producing an American edition of Maclean's. However, we know its influence was in the back rooms of senior civil servants, and as a result a terrible bill was imposed on the Canadian people. I know some of my colleagues disagree, but all that bill achieved was exactly what Maclean-Hunter intended. Time was driven out of Canada and is now making more money outside Canada from Canadians-three times more, I am told-than the largest amount it made in its 30 previous years inside Canada. These are the kinds of

lobbyists we will not ever get to register. They are in the back rooms.
Yes, it is the government now in power which will take the flack for what the lobbyists like Maclean-Hunter did in the . back rooms. It will always be the government in power that takes the blame. These key public service people-malcontents, power seekers, people open to inducements, will manipulate cabinet ministers, of whatever party, because they know what they are doing, and they do not have any responsibility to the public. They do what they do without being identified; they do it anonymously; and their mouthpiece becomes the cabinet minister. To me this is a personal embarrassment. Ministers are the people whom I feel are the most vulnerable when lobbyists join the support of their executive staffs. We-the elected representatives-then take the blame for what is done as a result. I consider those groups a menace, and their deeds are the signpost to the end of the road for democractic government, regardless of party. Even now there are some who quite openly say that we will not be here four years or eight years from now, but they are here forever.
I must stress that I do not want to offend all civil servants. I am impressed with most public servants. I think most are loyal and maintain their oath, but the malcontents, power seekers, and those who leave themselves open to inducements are the ones I am discussing here. I cannot understand why some of these things are happening. I cannot blame my own ministers, with whom I disagree on some issues. The Northland Navigation fiasco on the West Coast-the tragedy created almost as though by malice aforethought-is one case. What is happening with the CRTC and with cable companies which are not happy with the excessive incomes they are making now is another.
The cable companies want pay television so that they can get an extra $1.5 billion a year. They are manipulating the CRTC so that they can get converters into every home in the country. The situation in Vancouver is a case in point. The hon. member for Surrey-White Rock (Mr. Friesen), the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds) and myself went before the CRTC and fought this. The cable companies deliberately spread the word that we were racists, which is absolutely ridiculous. We fought the plan to take all the American network stations off the dial.
It is obvious to us now that the CRTC and the cable companies want them off so that people will be forced to buy converters. This way they will be able to get pay television into every home, and we will then have to pay for the programs we now get free. This is happening right now. We fought the CRTC and the cable group. They were lobbyists when they first tried to take American network stations off in January last year. We fought them when they took FM off without consultation with those who represented the people in the area.
It was forced back on when the Liberal caucus from B.C. went to the cabinet and raised a protest, along with the protest of our greatest lobby, our constituents. We protested so loudly that the FM decision was reversed.
January 28, 1977

When I talk about our French network stations I am not being racist. I am part of a minority group which knows about racism and the realities of racism. I am not talking about racism. I am talking about economics and realities. The last report of the bureau of measurement indicated that the listening audience to the French network at Vancouver is 400 at prime time, and 100 most of the day; it could be less, but that is the lowest measure possible.
The only time the French network has an audience of any size-1,300-is late at night, at about eleven o'clock, when the pornographic movies come on. The cable companies and the CRTC now plan to take channel 4 off the dial. Channel 4 is the most popular station out of Seattle. They want to substitute for channel 4 the French network station for the sake of 400 viewers. Those 400 viewers could get converters, but it is not profitable to sell pay-TV to only 400. They want the whole population of half a million in Vancouver to have converters so that they can charge for pay television. This is the kind of lobbying and manipulation within the public service that terrifies me.
An incident occurred in Burnaby, B.C., yesterday. Burnaby borders on my constituency. Perhaps hon. members on both sides of this House could learn something from the incident. A fire chief was selected through a proper competition. The deputies had the right to apply, and I expect that they did enter the competion. The best fire chief was chosen from outside the department. He was chosen by the elected representatives.
The deputies in the fire department immediately sent this man to Coventry. They would not co-operate, and their subordinates joined the fight against the new chief. Finally the mayor, Tom Constable, who is a trade union leader and, like myself, concerned about justice for the rank and file-he is a concerned person, and I think a member of the New Democratic Party-fired two deputies yesterday after a long and bitter struggle. Two more are to be fired. This action took place after this long and bitter struggle, after the fire chief was hired by the elected representatives and after the staff members refused to work. I suggest that it is time that these inside lobbies and the people who are manipulating hon. members on both sides of the House go the same way when we have any sign they are disloyal. If they are not working in the best interests of Canada but working for pressure groups with vested interests, we should start cleaning them out.
There has been talk here about blacklists. I do not care about blacklists. I want to talk about some people who came from Simon Fraser University. As a reporter, I knew them, and they were a meance to the university. They did not allow students free access to jobs or to classrooms. Some students lost part or all of their year of study. Yet these people were hired on the federal public service. I wonder why. Few of them I knew were capable of loyalty to the Canadian people. They were not loyal to their colleagues. I hope someone knows they are in the public service, and I hope that they were released if their continuing subversion was noted.
Lobbying
I agree with the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton with regard to a freedom of information bill. I believe we should have freedom of information, but as long as the public service does not want us to know what is going on in the back rooms, we will not have it.
The public servants had already made their decision to withdraw the subsidy in the case of Northland Navigation when they called a meeting. These are civil servants, not the government of Canada. They had already made their decision to withdraw the subsidy, but they said they had to hold the meeting in order to get some members of parliament off their backs.
The hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Baldwin) has cited incidents to me, and I have read about senior civil servants who have said that they do not want members of parliament interfering in their affairs; in other words, it is their country, they are running it, and members of parliament "should stay out of our business." I think it is time we cleaned them out.
I would like to say to hon. members opposite that I am well aware of the little brown envelopes coming to them containing information. I am well aware that civil servants are feeding hon. members opposite information with which they might try to tear this government down. I know that many hon. members opposite are beginning to get nervous because of the danger inherent in this. If those public servants are giving out this information now, they would give it to us if we were on the other side, if that ever came about. I do not know whether it is going to happen. I suppose it will happen some day because society always wants change, but I do not think it will happen soon, probably not for about 20 years.
To be very serious, these few people in the public service do not want democratic government; they want government by civil service. That would be the end of democracy and the start of rule from within by people who are not accountable to the public.
On November 30 in the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts I had my first insight of how we are simply rubber stamps for the people who seem to run this country. That sounds like a very negative way of handling this question of lobbying but I was very discouraged because I have to answer to my constituents-as we all do- for things that I know were not created by members on either side of this House. The estimates were before that committee in an amount around $59,000. A man named Bruce Donaldson of the government telephone agency appeared as a witness. The agency wanted to pay something like $38,000 for furniture. Without any reference to the committee it had increased the staff, at a time of restraint, by 40 people. They just bought the furniture-a fait accompli-and then came with the estimates to be passed.
The hon. member for Fundy-Royal (Mr. Fairweather), bemoaning the terrible telephone service the agency provided, was told that the equipment was very old and could not be replaced. Facetiously, I suggested they could have done what

Lobbying
they did with the furniture-simply buy the equipment and bring the account to us to be rubber stamped, and then the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) could take the blame for the government expenditure! That is the name of the game, Mr. Speaker. They do it, we rubber stamp it, and the Prime Minister takes the blame.
It does not matter what we call them-pressure groups, special interest groups, lobbyists-the name is interchangeable. Special interest groups will say they do not want to be called lobbyists, but the word does not change the fact. Spokesmen for unions, industry and large organizations like to pretend they speak for large numbers of people when all too often they have only had an executive meeting. They share the dialogue and then come and say they are speaking for 20,000, or 2'A million, or 20 million people.
As an example, Mr. Speaker, I have received letters from officers of the British Columbia Teachers' Federation protesting the treatment of Dr. Morgentaler. This came in a copy of a most, insulting letter to the Prime Minister of Canada, on BCTF letterhead. But I have yet to find one teacher in British Columbia-and I have shown this letter to many of them- who knew they were involved in this matter. They had the distinct impression their association was concerned about the major problem of education.
This is what worries me, Mr. Speaker. Are lobbyists really speaking for the mass of the people? Will registration of them make any difference? In the case of the cable company, I know that when we get through fighting for channel 4 we will have to fight them again and again on new issues. They will not stop until they win. Lobbyists have a single purpose; they are paid and all they have to do is work on one thing at a time. We have to work on many things and, while we are moving to our next problem, they are concentrating on the one. We cannot change the fact that they are working inside with the public service.
It should not be any comfort to the opposition that there are those who lobby with the aid of the public service-and I do not say all of the public service-in the name of nationalism, as we have seen for example with the television and magazine industry. Nationalism has been the device used for building the empires of the greedy. If this cable lobby succeeds then they could do it to any government, and elected representatives will not have control. One of the executives of the cable company stated that he hoped he could delay KOMO, Seattle's, replacement on channel 4; on the VHF dial by French network to a time just a month or two before the elections, so that he could bring the government down. I say if he could do it to us, he could do it to the opposition.
I should like to refer to lobbying in regard to the proposed gun law, Mr. Speaker. In Vancouver there is a very serious rapist, a frightening person whom the Calgary and Vancouver police feel has been involved in the rape of aged people, and is capable of murder. Bill C-83, the peace and security legislation, was introduced in this House last year. The person involved in those rapes is now free on the streets of Vancouver on mandatory parole. He had to be freed. Under the law it was

legal and his right on completing his sentence under existing law. He is now out on the streets on mandatory parole; the public is angry at us because we have no way of getting him and other dangerous people off the streets.
Recently some hon. members visited a penitentiary on the prairies, and there I talked to two prisoners in segregation cells, a 16 year old and an 18 year old who will be free in four or five months. Neither of them have any fear of death.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I should like to finish this point. Those two boys have said it does not mean anything to them to kill, and they probably will kill. They do not know why. They do not know anything else, and they are coming out in four or five months. If there had been co-operation for the passage of Bill C-83, which has provisions for dealing with dangerous offenders through indefinite sentences, we could have kept society safe from the Vancouver rapist and these two youngsters who have no sense of life and death. We would probably have prevented this rapist from being released on the mandatory parole that is now his legal entitlement.
I feel this is an important matter, Mr. Speaker, and we ought to work it out. I do not see how we can answer all the questions of the gun lobbys, the pro-life lobbys, the union lobbys who really do not represent the people. But my greatest concern is the inside lobby, Mr. Speaker, the group from within that is undermining democratic government.

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) and, if I may say so in the same breath, the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson), who have both had bills on the order paper on this general question of lobbying and who both made very able presentations in the House today.
I appreciate the thoughts and the examples given by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) on the subject, and the very interesting and thoughtful ideas we have just heard from the hon. member for Vancouver-Kings-way (Mrs. Holt). We have had a very useful discussion on the question of lobbying by people obviously interested in and knowledgeable about the subject. In addition, in past years the House had devoted many hours to an analysis of the validity of lobbying and the conduct of lobbyists.
If one searches back through the debates of this House, as I have done in examining the bill presented by the hon. member for Grenville-Carleton, one comes across repeated discussions of this topic. Many of these were prompted and promoted through private members' bills introduced by the former member from Surrey, British Columbia. The idea of lobbyists has been rather thoroughly canvassed on these occasions and I

think we have benefited by the discussion. I should like to refer to one occasion in particular, April 14, 1970. It was reported at page 5854 of the Commons Debates. This was in the course of one of the debates on a private members' bill of the former member for Surrey.
Barry Mather.

Mr. Mather was the gentleman who presented the subject on that occasion and, I gather from reports, on other occasions as well.
If I could, I would quote a passage from some of the debates at that particular time. However, I will not take the time of the House to do that. If hon. members are interested, I refer them to page 5854 of the Commons Debates where the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) was discussing the question of lobbying. He made some rather interesting points.
Lobbying
I would adopt at least a portion of his wording which has to do with the inequity of legislation of this kind.
The hon. member pointed out that it necessarily establishes separate classes within that broad group generally defined as lobbyists. It creates a basic inequity. Some would have to register, perhaps pay a fee and subject themselves to other restrictions. Others would not be subject to those restrictions even though their actions may be more sinister. I have serious doubts about the efficacy of this kind of proposal.
